title: Absolute Convergence and the Wiener Algebra

items.title: The Wiener algebra of the circle
items.strategy: With T = R/Z, normalized Haar measure, and e_k(x) = exp(2 pi i k x), define A(T) as the functions represented by an absolutely summable Fourier series and identify its norm with the l1 norm of its coefficient sequence. The uniformly convergent representative is part of the definition-level construction.

items.title: Absolute summability gives uniform Fourier synthesis
items.strategy: Apply the Weierstrass M-test to sum a_k e_k, then use termwise integration against e_-m and uniform convergence to recover its Fourier coefficients. This proves that the coefficient description in the definition is unambiguous.

items.title: The Wiener algebra is a Banach algebra
items.strategy: Transport completeness from l1(Z) through uniform Fourier synthesis. For multiplication, first prove the convolution formula for finite sums, pass to the uniform limits, and use the l1 convolution inequality to obtain the submultiplicative norm bound.

items.title: Weighted l2 Fourier decay implies absolute convergence
items.strategy: For s > 1/2, apply Cauchy--Schwarz to the nonzero coefficients using weights |k|^s, invoke convergence of sum over k nonzero of |k|^(-2s), and handle the zero coefficient separately.

items.title: A dyadic square-sum bound for Hölder functions
items.strategy: For f in C^alpha(T), choose a translation h comparable to N^(-1). Orthogonality for the finite frequency block bounds the block l2 norm by the L2 norm of f(.+h)-f, while |e_k(h)-1| is uniformly bounded below for N <= |k| < 2N. Hölder control then yields the N^(-2 alpha) square-sum estimate.

items.title: Bernstein's absolute-convergence theorem
items.strategy: Decompose the nonzero frequencies into dyadic annuli. On each annulus use Cauchy--Schwarz and the preceding square-sum bound; the resulting geometric series converges exactly when alpha > 1/2. State the result for C^alpha(T), 0 < alpha <= 1, under the page's normalized convention.

items.title: One L2 weak derivative implies absolute convergence
items.strategy: Use the later weak-derivative identity for Fourier coefficients and Parseval to put (k fhat(k)) in l2; then invoke weighted l2 decay with s = 1. The forward reference is deliberate: the weak-derivative definition belongs to PDE-11.

items.title: Interface to the Wiener lemma
items.strategy: Record, without restating or reproving it, that the exact inverse-closedness theorem for a nonvanishing member of A(T) is owned by FA-18. Explain that the Banach-algebra result here supplies its algebraic ambient setting.

items.title: Holomorphic functional calculus in the Wiener algebra
items.strategy: After the FA functional-calculus theorem is available, apply it to the unital Banach algebra A(T); formulate the corollary only for holomorphic functions on a neighborhood of the spectrum. Do not substitute a continuous functional calculus or use the Wiener lemma as a duplicate proof.

title: Absolute Convergence and the Wiener Algebra — Examples

items.title: A trigonometric polynomial belongs to the Wiener algebra
items.strategy: Its Fourier coefficient sequence has finite support, so its A(T) norm is a finite sum. Compute the norm as the sum of the moduli of the displayed coefficients.

items.title: An absolutely convergent Fourier series that is not twice continuously differentiable
items.strategy: For f(x) = sum over k nonzero of |k|^(-2)e_k(x), establish membership in A(T) by comparison. If f were C2, two integrations by parts would make the Fourier coefficients of f'' a nonzero constant for k nonzero, contradicting the Riemann--Lebesgue lemma.

items.title: Continuity does not imply absolute convergence
items.strategy: Present the source-supported existence statement of a continuous periodic function whose Fourier coefficient sequence is not in l1. Contrast it with the sufficient Hölder threshold without suggesting that every continuous function has this defect.

items.title: The Hölder-one-half endpoint can fail
items.strategy: Use Grafakos's cited lacunary series, together with the stated exponential-sum estimate, to obtain a function in Lambda^(1/2)(T) whose coefficients are not absolutely summable. Preserve the source's qualification that the exponential-sum estimate is not supplied in that exercise.

items.title: Wiener inversion needs nonvanishing
items.strategy: The polynomial 1 - e_1 belongs to A(T) but vanishes at 0 in T. It therefore cannot have a continuous, hence cannot have an A(T), pointwise reciprocal; this shows why the nonvanishing hypothesis is indispensable.
